transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because my sleep has just... fallen apart, really. I’m normally very disciplined about it—I have to be, with my work. I’m in board meetings, I’m expected to be sharp, and I’ve always been someone who can keep a routine.

But since my cousin died, I lie awake at night replaying that night over and over. And then even when I do fall asleep, I wake up at 3 or 4 in the morning with these scraps of hospital images in my head. Not even a full dream, just pieces of it, and then I’m wide awake again.

So I’ve been going into meetings feeling like I’ve only slept in pieces, if that makes sense. It’s not like me, and I thought I should talk to someone before it starts really affecting everything.
How long have you been experiencing these sleep problems since your cousin died?

It’s been about three weeks now. It started that same night—after the highway collision, when my cousin died. I remember thinking at first it was just the shock of that night, that maybe after a few days my body would settle down again, but it hasn’t really. So yes, roughly three weeks of sleeping badly, pretty much since then.
Have you been feeling sad or empty since your cousin's death?

Yes… but it’s a little hard to describe, because it hasn’t felt like normal sadness exactly. I mean, of course I know I’m grieving, and at the prayer gatherings I did what I was supposed to do—I greeted people, accepted condolences, sat with the family, said the right things. From the outside I probably looked composed.

But inside, there was this strange absence. Even when my nieces were trying to comfort me, holding my hand or leaning against me, I could respond properly, but I didn’t feel that warmth or relief you’d expect. It was almost like the affectionate part of me had gone quiet. Not that I don’t love them—I do—but I couldn’t really feel it in the moment. It felt empty in a very unsettling way.
Have you found yourself losing interest in activities that you normally enjoy?

I’m not sure I’d say that, exactly. I haven’t really been doing much for enjoyment in the usual sense, but it’s hard to separate what’s “loss of interest” from just… the circumstances.

I still recognize the things I usually like. I still think, yes, normally I’d enjoy reading, or cooking something proper, or going for a walk and clearing my head. But lately I haven’t really tested it much. Everything has felt interrupted, and I’ve been more focused on getting through the obligations in front of me.

So I wouldn’t say I’ve clearly stopped caring about those things. It’s more that I haven’t had much space for them, if that makes sense.
Do you find yourself thinking that you could have done something to prevent your cousin's death?

I… I don’t really know. I’ve gone over pieces of it in my head, of course, because that’s what you do when something terrible happens—you keep looking for some point where the story could have gone differently. But I can’t honestly say I have a clear belief that I personally could have prevented it.

There are moments where I wonder, “What if someone had called earlier?” or “What if plans had changed?” But it feels more like my mind trying to make sense of something awful than me truly thinking I had control over it. I wasn’t in a position where I can point to one action and say, “If I had done this, my cousin would still be alive.” I just… I don’t think I know how to answer it more definitely than that.
Do you feel guilty about your cousin's death?

Guilty… I don’t know if that’s the right word. I’ve asked myself that, actually, because people say that after a death, don’t they—“you feel guilty,” or “you blame yourself”—and I keep trying to see if that’s what’s happening in me.

I don’t feel like I’m sitting here thinking, “This was my fault.” I really don’t. I can’t point to something I did or didn’t do and say I caused it. But there are little flashes where I think, maybe I should have been more present, or maybe I should have known something, or maybe families are supposed to sense when something is wrong. And then I tell myself that’s not reasonable.

So… not guilt exactly. More confusion, maybe. A kind of uneasiness. But I wouldn’t say I feel guilty in a clear way.
Have you noticed any changes in your movement or activity level since your cousin's death, such as feeling restless or slowed down?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed anything very clear in that way. I mean, I wouldn’t say I’ve been pacing around constantly or unable to sit still, and I also wouldn’t say I feel physically slowed down in some dramatic way.

My routine has been a bit off, certainly, but that feels more like everything has been disrupted rather than my body moving differently, if that makes sense. I can still get up, get dressed, do the things I need to do. Maybe I’m not as efficient as I normally am, but I don’t know that it’s a movement or activity-level change exactly.

So… no, I don’t think I’ve noticed restlessness or being slowed down as a major thing. At least not in a way that stands out to me.
Have you lost any weight since your cousin's death?

I don’t think so. I mean, I haven’t been weighing myself every day or anything like that, so I can’t give you a precise answer in pounds. But my clothes don’t feel noticeably looser, and no one has commented that I look like I’ve lost weight.

I suppose things have been irregular in the way they tend to be when you’re upset and distracted, but in terms of actual weight loss, I haven’t noticed anything significant. If there has been any change, it’s not something that’s stood out to me.
Have you stopped doing things you usually enjoy since your cousin's death?

I think… yes, in a way, though it’s not as simple as, “I used to like gardening and now I don’t,” or something neat like that. It’s more that when I’m in situations where I would normally feel some comfort or warmth, I just don’t seem to be able to reach it.

For example, at the prayer gatherings, everyone was being kind, and I knew what I was supposed to do. I greeted people, thanked them, sat with the family, did all the proper things. And my nieces tried to comfort me—hugging me, sitting close, saying things that were genuinely loving. I could recognize that it was loving. I could even respond appropriately, I think. But inside, there was just… nothing warm coming back. No relief, no softness.

That has been the strangest part. I haven’t necessarily stopped showing up for things, but I feel like the part of me that would usually take in affection or feel touched by it has gone quiet. Like I’m behaving correctly on the outside, but I’m not getting the feeling that’s supposed to go with it.
Have you felt like you're getting any pleasure out of the things you're still doing?

Not really, no. Or… I suppose I should say, I’m still doing some of the things. I’m still showing up, still speaking to people, still doing what’s expected of me. At the prayer gatherings, for example, I was there, I was participating, I was thanking people, accepting their condolences, sitting with family. From the outside I probably looked composed enough.

But I didn’t feel any real comfort from it. That’s the part that unsettles me. People were being kind, and I knew they were being kind. My nieces were especially sweet—they would sit close to me, hug me, try to reassure me—and normally that would soften me. I would feel touched by it, or at least feel some warmth.

Instead it was like I was going through the correct motions and nothing was landing inside. No relief, no warmth, no little moment of feeling better. I could recognize that something loving was happening, but I couldn’t really take any pleasure or comfort from it. It’s almost like that affectionate part of me has gone quiet for now.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in things you used to find enjoyable?

Yes… I think I have, though it feels less like I’ve consciously “lost interest” and more like the enjoyment just doesn’t reach me.

At the prayer gatherings, for example, I was doing everything I normally would. I was greeting people, thanking them, sitting with the family, letting people come up and say kind things. And my nieces were trying so hard to comfort me—hugging me, staying near me, saying sweet things—and normally that would mean something to me emotionally. I would feel warmth from that, or at least a little relief.

But I just found myself behaving properly, almost automatically, while inside there was no real warmth. No comfort. No softening. It was like I could see that people were being loving, and I could respond the way I was supposed to, but the feeling part of it wasn’t there. Almost like the affectionate part of me had gone quiet. So yes, I suppose I haven’t been getting enjoyment or comfort from things I usually would.
Do you feel like you've stopped wanting to do things that you used to enjoy?

Yes… I think so, although it feels a little complicated. I haven’t necessarily stopped doing everything, because I’m still the sort of person who shows up and does what’s expected. At the prayer gatherings, I was there, I was speaking to people, thanking them, sitting where I was supposed to sit, letting people come close.

But wanting to do it, or feeling drawn to it in any comforting way… no, not really. It felt more like I was performing the part of myself who knows how to behave. Even when my nieces tried to comfort me, and they were so sweet—hugging me, sitting beside me, trying to make me feel less alone—I could tell it was loving, but I didn’t feel that warmth inside that I normally would. There was no relief from it.

So I suppose it’s not that I refuse to do things. It’s more that the wanting, the pleasure, the affectionate response… it’s gone quiet. Almost like I’m present on the outside, but not really able to receive anything good from it.
Do you feel like you have no interest in doing things that you used to enjoy?

Yes… though I keep hesitating over the word “interest,” because I’m still doing things. I’m still present. I still know what I’m supposed to do.

At the prayer gatherings, for instance, I went through all of it properly. I sat with people, spoke to them, accepted their kindness, thanked them. I wasn’t refusing anyone or shutting everyone out in some obvious way. But inside, it felt very flat. Like I was there as a body, as a role, but not really receiving anything.

And with my nieces… that’s what really made me notice it. They were trying so hard to comfort me—sitting close, hugging me, being gentle with me—and normally that would touch me. I would feel some warmth, some tenderness, even if I was sad. But I didn’t feel that. I could see that they loved me, and I could respond correctly, but there was no relief inside. No little softening.

So yes, I think the interest, or maybe the ability to feel comfort from things I normally care about, feels almost absent right now. It’s as if that affectionate part of me has gone quiet.
Do you feel like the things that used to bring you pleasure just don't feel enjoyable anymore?

Yes… yes, that’s probably the clearest way to put it. Things that should feel comforting, or at least meaningful, just don’t seem to reach me the way they normally would.

At the prayer gatherings, I knew people were being kind. I could see it. I was answering them properly, thanking them, letting them sit with me, doing all the things one does. And on the outside I must have looked composed enough, because I know how to behave in those situations. But inside, there wasn’t much there. No warmth, no real comfort, no sense of being soothed.

And when my nieces tried to comfort me… that was especially strange. They were so sweet, and normally I would feel that deeply. I would feel touched by it, even if I was upset. But this time I just sort of noticed it happening. I knew they loved me, I knew they were trying to help, and I responded to them, but I didn’t feel the relief or tenderness I expected to feel.

So yes, things that used to bring me comfort or pleasure don’t feel enjoyable right now. It’s like that affectionate part of me has gone quiet, and I’m just going through the motions.
Do you feel like the things you used to enjoy are now feeling empty or without pleasure to you?

Yes… empty is exactly the word, I think. Not empty in the sense that I don’t understand what’s happening around me, or that I don’t appreciate what people are trying to do. I do understand it. I can see it. I can behave properly in response to it.

But inside, it just doesn’t land. During the prayer gatherings, I was there, doing what I was supposed to do—sitting with people, speaking when I needed to, accepting their condolences, thanking them. Outwardly I think I seemed appropriate, maybe even composed. But there wasn’t that feeling of being held up by it, if that makes sense. There was no warmth coming back to me from the kindness.

And with my nieces, that was especially painful to notice. They were trying so hard to comfort me, and I love them, I know I do. Normally their affection would soften me immediately. But I just… I behaved the way I should, hugged them, let them be close, said the right things, but inside there was no real relief. It was like the affectionate part of me had gone quiet, or gone numb somehow.

So yes, things that should feel comforting or meaningful feel very hollow right now. I’m present for them, but I don’t feel pleasure or comfort from them the way I normally would.
How long have you been feeling this emptiness or lack of emotional response?

About three weeks now. It started that night—since the night my cousin died in the highway collision.

I keep thinking maybe it will lift after a few days, or after each prayer gathering, or after I’ve spoken to enough people, but it hasn’t really changed. It’s been there more or less the whole time, this flatness, like I can recognize what should matter emotionally but I can’t quite feel it. So yes… about three weeks.
Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure from almost all activities most of the time?

Yes… I think so. I mean, I don’t know if I can honestly say “every single activity,” because I haven’t exactly been testing myself, if that makes sense. But most of the things that should bring some comfort or warmth just feel very muted, almost absent.

The clearest examples are still the prayer gatherings and my nieces. At the gatherings, I know people were being loving and respectful, and I was doing what I was supposed to do—speaking to people, thanking them, accepting their kindness. But inside there was no real warmth coming back to me. It was like I could recognize the shape of comfort without actually feeling comfort.

And with my nieces, that was the part that made me notice it the most. They tried so sweetly to comfort me, and normally that would touch me deeply. I would feel softened by it. But I found myself just behaving properly—hugging them, responding to them, letting them be near me—while inside I felt no relief, no tenderness rising up the way it usually would. Almost as if the affectionate part of me had just gone quiet.

So yes, most of the time, the things that should feel good or comforting don’t really feel pleasurable right now. I’m participating, but I’m not feeling it.
Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure from almost all activities most of the time?

Yes… I know I’ve said this, but that really is how it feels. It’s not that I don’t recognize what should be comforting or meaningful. I do. I can see people are being kind, I can understand that my nieces are trying to love me through it, and I respond the way I’m supposed to.

But inside, there’s just very little there. At the prayer gatherings, I was sitting with everyone, accepting condolences, thanking people, doing all the proper things. And yet I didn’t feel that warmth I would expect from being surrounded by people who care. It was almost like I was watching myself receive comfort without actually feeling comforted.

And with my nieces, that bothered me the most. They were so gentle with me, trying to be close and reassure me, and normally that would touch me immediately. But I hugged them and spoke to them, and inside there wasn’t that relief or softness. It felt like the affectionate part of me had gone quiet.

So yes, most of the time, the things that should bring me pleasure or comfort just don’t seem to reach me right now.
Have you had any days in the past three weeks where you felt somewhat better and were able to enjoy things or feel a little pleasure?

Not really, no. I mean… there may have been moments where I was distracted or where I was functioning a little better on the outside, but I wouldn’t call it enjoyment exactly.

Even during the prayer gatherings, when people were around me and saying kind things, I knew it should have felt comforting. I could see that it was loving, and I behaved the way I should—thanked people, sat with them, accepted their sympathy. But inside I didn’t feel that warmth or relief you’d expect.

And with my nieces, that was the hardest to understand. They were trying so sweetly to comfort me, and I went through the motions of being close to them, hugging them, responding to them… but I didn’t really feel softened by it. It was almost like the affectionate part of me had gone quiet.

So no, I don’t think I’ve had a day where I truly felt better in that sense. Maybe brief moments of being occupied, but not real pleasure.
Do you feel like you're depressed?

I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I know I feel very low, and flat, and not like myself. If you’re asking whether I wake up and think, “I’m depressed,” I don’t know that I’ve been labeling it that way.

It feels more like… something in me has shut down, or gone numb. I’m not crying all day in the way people might imagine, but I’m also not really feeling normal sadness either. It’s more muted than that, like I’m moving through things and responding to people, but I’m not fully inside my own life.

So… maybe? I don’t know. I can say I don’t feel okay. But I’m not sure whether what I’m feeling is depression, or shock, or just my mind trying to get through it.
